card.title: Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crystallization and crystal growth; water of crystallization

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Three solids, one gradient of water vapour. **Efflorescent** hydrates sit above the air's moisture pressure and bleed their lattice water out — washing soda and Glauber's salt powder themselves on the shelf. **Hygroscopic** solids sip moisture and stay whole — quicklime, silica gel, P₂O₅, the desiccator's residents.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Efflorescent substances lose their water of crystallisation to the atmosphere; deliquescent substances absorb moisture from the atmosphere and dissolve in it."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The desiccator*** — a glass vessel over silica gel or CaCl₂ keeps tongs-dry samples and cools red-hot crucibles without them gaining weight — humidity control by deliquescence.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: One vapour-pressure gradient explains all three behaviours — the same rule that drives evaporation (topic 47) drives every drying agent and every crumbling hydrate.  ·  Efflorescent: hydrate loses lattice water (VP of hydrate > air moisture): Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O. Hygroscopic: absorbs moisture, stays solid: CaO, silica gel, P₂O₅, conc. H₂SO₄. Deliquescent: absorbs and dissolves (solution VP < air moisture): CaCl₂·6H₂O, MgCl₂·6H₂O, ZnCl₂, FeCl₃, KOH. Water of crystallisation: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue→white test), FeSO₄·7H₂O, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, gypsum 2H₂O.…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Solids That Fight the Air Some solids stay dry forever, some soak the air dry, some crumble into solution without a drop of water added. Efflorescent, hygroscopic and deliquescent solids sit at three points on one water-vapour gradient — and knowing which is which saves experiments, reagents and exam marks.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The three behaviours - **Efflorescent:** a hydrated solid that **loses** its water of crystallisation to the air at room temperature, crusting to a powder. Examples: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (washing soda), Na₂SO₄·10H₂O (Glauber's salt), CuSO₄·5H₂O (partially, to the trihydrate), MgSO₄·7H₂O.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Direction mnemonic: "efflorescent = exhalation (loses); deliquescent = drinks and dissolves; hygroscopic = humects (damp only)". Waters: blue vitriol 5, green 7, washing soda 10, gypsum 2. Blue→white→blue = CuSO₄ water test.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Roads are salted with NaCl/CaCl₂ in winter partly because deliquescence keeps a brine film active below 0 °C — the same chemistry that ruins untightened salt bags.

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why washing soda crumbles and CaCl₂ puddles - Na₂CO₃·10H₂O's hydrate vapour pressure exceeds the water vapour normally in air, so it effloresces to the monohydrate/powder. CaCl₂·6H₂O's saturated solution has vapour pressure below air's moisture content, so water flows inward until the salt dissolves completely — a puddle of concentrated…  ·  ## 5. rows.text: Classify: anhydrous CaCl₂, washing soda, silica gel, FeCl₃, gypsum — with reasons.  ·  Why does a bottle of KOH left open end up half-full of liquid?  ·  Design a test to show that gypsum contains water of crystallisation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Hygroscopic vs deliquescent — the solution decides:** both absorb water; only the deliquescent salt *dissolves* in what it absorbs. CaO absorbs (stays solid, becomes Ca(OH)₂ by reaction); CaCl₂·6H₂O dissolves.  ·  **Efflorescence needs a hydrate:** anhydrous solids cannot effloresce — there is no lattice water to lose.  ·  **Water of crystallisation is not "wetness":** it is stoichiometric, structural water — CuSO₄·5H₂O is a dry, powdery crystal holding five waters per formula unit inside its lattice.
